title: The eye is an ocean
hookLine: the eye is an ocean for a person, its waves are forms (SN 35.228)

cards: You open your phone to check the time. Forty minutes later you surface, a little dazed, holding a stranger's vacation photos and a pair of shoes you didn't need in your cart. You didn't decide to go under.
A current pulled, then another, and you went with it. People in the Buddha's day didn't have phones, but they knew the feeling.
In one short discourse of the Connected Sayings, he takes the word for the vast, dangerous sea and moves it somewhere much closer.

teach.h: THAT'S JUST A GREAT MASS OF WATER
teach.b: SN 35.228 begins with a correction. The untaught person says, the ocean, the ocean. But that's not the ocean in the training of the noble ones, the Buddha says.
That's just a great mass of water. Then the real ocean. The eye, monks, is the ocean for a person.
Its surge is made of forms, the sights that come at it.

teach.h: THE EYE IS THE OCEAN, FORMS ITS SURGE
teach.b: Whoever withstands that surge of forms has crossed the ocean of the eye, with its waves and whirlpools, its sharks and its demons. Then the rest. The ear is an ocean, its surge is sounds.
The nose, smells. The tongue, tastes. The body, touches.

The mind is an ocean, and its surge is ideas and thoughts. Each has the same dangers. A closing verse says that one who has crossed this ocean, so hard to cross, has gone beyond, and stands on dry ground.
The dangers are chosen carefully. Waves knock you over: a sudden sight that grabs you. Whirlpools pull you round and round, like the one in the Itivuttaka a few weeks back.
Sharks and demons bite: some sights and sounds really do hurt. None of it says the senses are bad.
You need eyes to cross a street.
The teaching is about the surge, the pull of what comes at the senses, and whether you get swept along. Withstanding is the word. Not closing the eyes.

how: Buddhist monastics practice restraint of the senses, guarding the eyes and ears in daily life, and many lay meditators practice noting sights and sounds as they arise without being carried off by them.

o: a flood that sweeps the world away
the ocean, each sense with its surge
a river that leads to the far shore

p: the ocean in the noble training

s: SN 35.228 says the eyes should be kept closed
it speaks of withstanding the surge of forms, not of closing the eyes.
each of the six senses is called an ocean
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, each with its own surge.
the ocean of the senses has sharks and demons in it
along with waves and whirlpools, as dangers to cross.

games.q: the Buddha says the eye is an ocean, and forms are its surge. how do you cross it?
o: dive in and enjoy the waves.
games.why: whoever withstands the surge of forms has crossed the ocean of the eye, with its waves, whirlpools, sharks and demons.

practice: Choose one sense for this sit, hearing is a good one, and let sounds come: traffic, a fridge, a voice, your own breath, each one a wave. Notice the tug that comes with some of them, toward a story, a judgment, a memory.
When you feel it, don't fight; stay where you are, afloat, and let the wave pass under you.

wordCard.voice: Samudda. The Pali word for the ocean, the image in SN 35.228: each sense is an ocean and its objects are the surge, with waves, whirlpools and sharks; whoever withstands it has crossed. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samudda: the ocean, the sea. SN 35.228 is the Samudda Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: feel for the current. The senses aren't the trouble; the surge is. Day six hundred fifty-three, done.
